doc.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998

chapter: Freelance years and The Loud Minority
title: 'Controlled chaos' and his first professional band
summary: The big band played loudly, he called it controlled confusion and says it was meant to swing, not be revolutionary.

blocks.x: And you guys did play loud, too.
Yeah, we lived up to our name man, that’s a fact. We definitely were telling the truth about who we were.
Was it a form of controlled chaos at some of your—
Did you hear me use that expression?
Yes. I use that expression sometimes.
Well I’ve read and I’ve heard some of the music and I mean up to 25 musicians at some point—
Yeah, I used to call it controlled chaos.
No kidding. I may have read that. It could be I read that.
I don’t know if it ever appeared in print but I used to announce it publicly.
We’re about to bring you an hour of controlled chaos. Oh no, I called it controlled confusion, that’s what it was, controlled confusion.

Which is pretty much the same. But now the music wasn’t meant to be revolutionary in nature, I just wanted to swing that’s all. I wanted to play some good music that everybody liked, music to listen to. It wasn’t wanting to — this is for black folks only, or this is for white folks only — this is for everybody, anybody who likes this music is free to listen and free to pay admission, come in. So but The Loud Minority, that title stood for something.
Was this your first experience as a band leader per se?
Well, as a professional, yes. My first experience as a band leader came as my senior year of high school when I had the 12-piece.
Oh that’s right, way back there.
A band of kids, high school age. And I wasn’t much of a leader, but for that year I was the man. So this, yeah, this was my first experience as a real, as a professional.
